cells.tense: The weight is here now, and you are still under it.
cells.act: stay in contact while it is hard
cells.ask: With someone who is carrying something heavy, stay in touch through the hard part this week. Don't fix it, don't lift it, don't take it onto yourself. And let your own weight rest on your own feet while you do.
cells.core:
The weight is here, and it hasn't flattened you. You can bear what has to be borne and hold it without squeezing — the tiredness moves through and you keep your shape, and the pressure doesn't turn you hard at the edges. That isn't rigidity. It's a body that can take load and stay soft, and it's doing that right now, whether or not anyone notices.

Someone close to you is carrying something this week. Sit with them in it instead of fixing it — don't lift it, don't hand them a solution, don't put it on your own shoulders — and let your own two feet hold your own weight while you're there. Staying through the hard part, once, on purpose, with one person, is what shows you what's already yours.
cells.sheetLine: You can hold what's heavy and still stay soft at the edges.
cells.verb: Bearing what has to be borne without hardening around it
cells.place: Where the body takes the load before anything is decided

cells.tense: You are bracing already for a weight that hasn't arrived yet.
cells.act: let an exchange flow both ways
cells.ask: When help or thanks comes your way, take it without matching it right away. Let one turn run one way and the next run the other, and keep no tally.
cells.core:
You're bracing for something that hasn't arrived. Where holding is needed, the grip has tightened past what the moment asks — the same strength that used to carry the load now spends itself on the next one, and what was steady has started to feel like holding on. From inside, it feels like being ready. From the other side of the door, it looks like nothing can get in.

Letting an exchange move both ways is the way back. When something is offered — help, thanks, someone taking a turn — take it and don't match it straight away. Let one exchange go one way and the next go the other, and keep no count of either. You're not out of proportion; you've overcorrected, and one unmeasured turn puts the measure back.
cells.sheetLine: The grip has tightened past what the moment is asking.
cells.verb: Bearing what has to be borne without hardening around it
cells.place: Where the body takes the load before anything is decided

cells.tense: The pressure came, and you were somewhere else when it landed.
cells.act: put it down and leave your hands empty a while
cells.ask: Pick something you've been carrying that no longer needs carrying, set it down on purpose, and let your hands be still a while. Not by dropping it — by laying it down and leaving it there.
cells.core:
The pressure came, and something in you went elsewhere. Where weight has to be borne, bearing it stopped being something you do and became something that reads as already done to you. What you can carry is still yours. It just went quiet, and nothing new is getting through while you wait at a threshold that's already behind you.

What comes back through is release, not more effort. Choose something you've been carrying that doesn't need carrying anymore, lay it down deliberately, and let your hands be still for a while. Not dropping it — setting it down with your own hands and walking away from it. Hands remember how to be empty faster than thinking does, and that's what brings you back to the pressure you're actually under.
cells.sheetLine: Hands remember empty, and that's the way back.
cells.verb: Bearing what has to be borne without hardening around it
cells.place: Where the body takes the load before anything is decided

cells.tense: You carry the weight and don't count it as anything you did.
cells.act: move toward the thing you actually want
cells.ask: Think of what you actually want, not what would help someone and not what is owed. Take a small step toward it, and tell nobody. The step is the whole of it.
cells.core:
The bearing is happening, and you wouldn't call it bearing. You take the weight when it comes and you hand the credit to the day, to the circumstances, to anyone but you — the strength in the scene is treated as the scene's, not yours. What you can hold is not a stranger's gift. It's yours, and it has been doing its work while you looked elsewhere for the author of it.

Wanting is the way back to seeing it. Choose something you actually want, not something that would help someone and not something owed, and take a small step toward it. Tell nobody about the step. It's yours in a way the bearing has felt like it belonged to circumstances, and one plainly yours move is how the strength becomes something you can name.
cells.sheetLine: The strength you don't count is still yours, still holding.
cells.verb: Bearing what has to be borne without hardening around it
cells.place: Where the body takes the load before anything is decided

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that the person's steadiness is felt as a floor by others — the record says the capacity is holding under pressure, not how it lands on anyone else, so I keep that to what the person's own bearing does and let any effect stay theirs to confirm. A reader could rightly say they have no choice about holding, that it isn't a capacity they'd claim, which is why the Too Little ask never pushes effort into the empty seat and hands them release instead. The ask survives being wrong: noticing what stops being needed, letting one thing go on purpose, turning toward one wanted thing all teach something even if the read misses. The sentence that serves me more than them is any line about a role others lean on, so I've cut that and left the bearing in their own hands.
